newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: OSCE warns Belarus on democracy ahead of summit.
newsitem.headline: OSCE warns Belarus on democracy ahead of summit.

text.p: Europe's security organisation issued a stern warning to Belarus on Saturday ahead of a major summit, saying it was seriously concerned by the way democracy was moving in the former Soviet republic.

The 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) said it would look at ways the body can help Belarus overcome what it called "its institutional crisis" at the summit which opens on Monday.

Beyond the diplomatic language, diplomatic sources said many member nations were seriously worried about President Alexander Lukashenkos moves to consolidate his autocratic rule through a recent referendum in his standoff with parliament.
Swiss Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti, the OSCE chairman-in-office, said it was his duty to ensure that the organisations democratic principles, to which Belarus had agreed, were fully respected.
Cotti sent OSCE Secretary-General Giancarlo Aragona to Minsk this week to meet Lukashenko and the heads of Belarus supreme council and constitutional court.

"The report of the secretary-general that the president is implementing the results of the referendum gives us great concern about the democratic development in Belarus," Cotti said in a statement issued in Lisbon.
His statement recalled that the OSCE's "troika" -- currently made up of Switzerland, Hungary and Denmark -- had already labelled the referendum as "illegitimate".

Lukashenko, who will attend the two-day summit in Portugal, has been trying to shut down the parliament following his victory last weekend in the referendum, condemned by Western nations as an unconstitutional grab for power.
Diplomats say many leaders from the OSCE, which groups the United States, Canada and all European states, were expected to criticise him during the Lisbon meeting.
Cotti said a team of OSCE legal experts had reported that constitutional procedures for the referendum were not followed.

Russia, which has not openly criticised the referendum, may in return win backing from Lukashenko if it raises its concerns over NATOs planned eastward expansion at the summit -- concerns shared by Belarus.

A senior member of the U.S. delegation in Lisbon said NATO members intended to focus on adapting a pact on European conventional arms cuts and steer clear of any talk about the alliance's plans to take on new members.

The summit was expected to authorise new negotiations in Vienna next year on adapting and extending the Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty signed in 1990 between NATO and the former Warsaw Pact.
"We recognise that the treaty as it stands is an important cornerstone of European security, but it no longer corresponds to the state of play," the U.S. delegation official said.
"The United States is very much behind the modernisation negotiations," he added.

Diplomatic sources said it was hoped the go-ahead for what would largely be a renegotiation of the CFE pact would be enough to defuse any potential dispute at the summit over NATO's expansion into central and eastern Europe.
But the OSCEs open criticism of Belarus may be a further cause of friction, and one diplomatic source raised doubt over whether Lukashenko would attend the summit and risk a diplomatic dressing-down.

Diplomats in London said on Friday Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, whose country currently holds the European Union presidency, may meet Lukashenko at the summit in Lisbon to express the EU's displeasure and concern.
